How Apple used Google's help to train its AI models
Google has been building TPUs for roughly 10 years, and has publicly discussed two flavors of its fifth-generation chips that can be used for AI training; the performance version of the fifth generation offers performance competitive with Nvidia H100 AI chips, Google said.
By Max A. Cherney
SAN FRANCISCO: On stage on Monday CEO Tim Cook's Apple announced a splashy deal with OpenAI to include its powerful artificial intelligence model as a part of its voice assistant, Siri.
But in the fine print of a technical document Apple published after the event, the company makes clear that Alphabet's Google has emerged as another winner in the Cupertino, California, company's quest to catch up in AI.
To build Apple's foundation AI models, the company's engineers used its own framework software with a range of hardware, specifically its own on-premise graphics processing units (GPUs) and chips available only on Google's cloud called tensor processing units (TPUs).
Google has been building TPUs for roughly 10 years, and has publicly discussed two flavors of its fifth-generation chips that can be used for AI training; the performance version of the fifth generation offers performance competitive with Nvidia H100 AI chips, Google said.
Google announced at its annual developer conference that a sixth generation will launch this year.
The processors are designed specifically to run AI applications and train models, and Google has built cloud computing hardware and software platform around them.
Apple and Google did not immediately return requests for comment.
Apple did not discuss the extent to which it relied on Google's chips and software compared with hardware from Nvidia or other AI vendors.
But using Google's chips typically requires a client to purchase access to them through its cloud division, much in the same way customers buy computing time from Amazon.com's AWS or Microsoft's Azure.

title: US weighs more limits on China's access to AI chips: Report - ET Telecom
text:
- Devices

US weighs more limits on China's access to AI chips: Report
The United States has been working to limit Beijing's access to advanced AI chips, such as those designed by leader Nvidia, through tightened trade restrictions amid fears that China may use the technology to bolster its military.
The Biden administration is considering further restrictions on China's access to chip technology used for artificial intelligence, Bloomberg News reported on Tuesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The measures being discussed would limit China's ability to use a cutting-edge chip architecture known as gate all-around, or GAA, the report said.
GAA is a type of transistor architecture that helps improve chip performance and reduces power consumption.
The United States has been working to limit Beijing's access to advanced AI chips, such as those designed by leader Nvidia, through tightened trade restrictions amid fears that China may use the technology to bolster its military.
With the scope of the potential rule still being determined, it is not clear when officials will make a final decision, the report said.
The rule is not yet finalized after industry officials criticized the first version as overly broad, the report said, adding that it is unclear whether the ban would restrict China's ability to develop its own GAA chips or seek to block U.S. chipmakers and other overseas companies from selling their products to Chinese firms.
Leading semiconductor firms including Nvidia, Intel and Advanced Micro Devices, along with chip manufacturers Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing and Samsung are aiming to start mass production of chips with the GAA design within the next year, according to the report.
The companies did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment, while the U.S. Department of Commerce declined to comment.
Stricter restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductors to China have already hampered chipmakers' position, with companies such as Intel and Qualcomm saying their sales would take a hit after the U.S. revoked some of their export licenses for a customer in China.
The Bloomberg report also said there have been some early-stage discussions about limiting exports of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) chips.
HBM chips, such as those made by South Korea's SK Hynix and Micron Technology, help speed up AI applications and are used by companies like Nvidia.

title: Oracle expects double-digit revenue growth for fiscal 2025 on strong AI demand - ET Telecom
text:
- Enterprise Services
- 2 min read
Oracle expects double-digit revenue growth for fiscal 2025 on strong AI demand
"I expect that each successive quarter should grow faster than the previous quarter - as OCI (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) capacity begins to catch up with demand," CEO Safra Catz said.
By Zaheer Kachwala
Oracle on Tuesday forecast revenue for fiscal 2025 to grow in double digits, above analysts' estimates, indicating strong demand for its AI-powered cloud services, sending the company's shares up 9% after the bell.
The company also announced a partnership with ChatGPT-maker OpenAI and Google Cloud to extend its own cloud infrastructure to customers.
"I expect that each successive quarter should grow faster than the previous quarter - as OCI (Oracle Cloud Infrastructure) capacity begins to catch up with demand," CEO Safra Catz said.
"In Q4 alone, Oracle signed over 30 AI sales contracts totaling more than $12.5 billion, including one with OpenAI to train ChatGPT in Oracle Cloud."
AI investments play a crucial role in Oracle's efforts to catch up with cloud giants such as Microsoft, which is seeing rapid growth of its own Azure cloud due to its tie-up with OpenAI.
Oracle has also spent billions of dollars on hardware from chip giant Nvidia.
The company's total revenue grew 3% to $14.29 billion in the fourth quarter, but missed LSEG estimates of $14.55 billion.
"In the cloud market, Oracle is doing well as the fourth-largest provider, but that business has to grow far bigger to help overall growth achieve double digits," said Gil Luria, research analyst at D.A. Davidson.
Oracle reported total revenue growth of 6% for fiscal 2024. For FY25, analysts expect 9% growth.
The company expects first-quarter revenue to grow between 5% and 7%, while analysts estimate a 7.6% rise.
"In Q3 and Q4, Oracle signed the largest sales contracts in our history, driven by enormous demand for training AI large language models in Oracle Cloud," Catz said.
Remaining performance obligations - the most popular measure of booked revenue - came at $98 billion in the fourth quarter, up 44% from a year ago.
It posted adjusted earnings per share of $1.63 per share, compared with estimates of $1.65 per share.

title: Not many investors enthused by Apple's 'AI for the rest of us' plan - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet

Not many investors enthused by Apple's 'AI for the rest of us' plan
Apple is making a high-stakes bid to catch up with rivals in the booming AI market. After falling behind peers like Google and Microsoft, it is counting on a streamlined interface - and loyal customer base - to regain ground.
Apple took the wraps off long-awaited new artificial intelligence features, including a partnership with OpenAI, betting that a personalised and understated approach to the technology will win over customers.
A new AI platform called Apple Intelligence was the highlight of the company's Worldwide Developers Conference presentation on Monday, which also included updates to the iPhone maker's operating systems. The technology will help summarise text, create original images and retrieve the most relevant data when users need it. The push also includes a revamped version of Siri, the company's digital assistant.
Investors gave a tepid reaction to the event - a not-uncommon reaction when Apple debuts long-anticipated new features. The shares declined about 0.7% in premarket trading on Tuesday before New York exchanges opened. The stock had closed down 1.9% to $193.12, leaving it little changed for the year. Shares of some key Apple suppliers also sank following the event.
Apple is making a high-stakes bid to catch up with rivals in the booming AI market. After falling behind peers like Google and Microsoft, it is counting on a streamlined interface - and loyal customer base - to regain ground.
"This is a moment we've been working toward for a long time," Senior vice president Craig Federighi, who oversees software engineering, said at the event. He described Apple Intelligence as "AI for the rest of us," alluding to an old slogan about the Mac computer. The partnership with OpenAI will let customers access ChatGPT via Siri at no extra cost. Apple Intelligence will begin rolling out later this year, but some features won't come until next year.
Shares of Alphabet, Google's parent company, spiked as much as 1.5% during Apple's keynote on Monday but were little changed at the close.
Suppliers' stocks slide
However, an overall lukewarm response to Apple's new AI features sank shares of some of the company's key Asian suppliers.
South Korea's LG Innotek Co tumbled as much as 9.5%, the most since September 2022, while China's Luxshare Precision Industry Co fell 4.1%. Both companies get more than 70% of their sales from Apple, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Analysts said the event to introduce the Apple Intelligence contained no big surprises, and would fail to alter the downbeat outlook for iPhone shipments this year.

title: AI is making robots smarter, they’ll need boundaries - ET Telecom
text:
- Internet
- 5 min read
AI is making robots smarter, they’ll need boundaries
The AI applications now offered on mobile robots are for simple tasks, but they will only become more complex over time. Teradyne Inc., which owns Universal Robots and Mobile Industrial Robots, sells a mobile pallet jack armed with five cameras that give it “sight” and a Nvidia chip that helps it “think” how best to pick up a pallet, even if it sits crooked or is damaged.
Artificial intelligence is sweeping across the economy. It’s showing up in the stock market with Nvidia’s meteoric rise, and the marketing blitz around AI is inescapable, whether from software providers peddling the promise of harnessed data to golf-club makers trumpeting an AI design. Narrow AI is now a real tool, and companies are figuring out how to deploy it.
Generative AI, virtual assistants and self-driving vehicles are some early use cases of the technology. Workers are being freed from tedious data-entry tasks such as extracting pertinent information from an email to fill an order and send a receipt. Software can scoop up financial data from public filings more quickly than a human and provide an instant synopsis. Most of this revolution is taking place in offices on company computers.
Where AI meets the physical world — and creates the potential for conflicts — is in manufacturing and logistics. Robots are already roaming factory and warehouse floors, and AI will make them smarter and more agile. As is usually the case with new technology, the military is prodding innovation. This marriage of AI and robots will require special rules to keep them constrained by humans, especially as these mobile machines move beyond the confines of a factory and become more prevalent in the service economy.
The AI applications now offered on mobile robots are for simple tasks, but they will only become more complex over time. Teradyne Inc., which owns Universal Robots and Mobile Industrial Robots, sells a mobile pallet jack armed with five cameras that give it “sight” and a Nvidia chip that helps it “think” how best to pick up a pallet, even if it sits crooked or is damaged.
The industry is in the early stages of producing general-purpose robots that will be able to accept verbal commands and process them into the code needed to carry out a specific task. While industrial robots programmed for repetitive tasks will always have their place, the versatility of general-purpose robots will make them popular if manufacturers drive down the price to make them competitive with hourly workers. Formic Technologies Inc. leases industrial robots to companies and offers one that stacks boxes on a pallet for about $15 an hour with maintenance included. AI can already write code from a process-flow diagram that spells out each step of a task with boxes and arrows. It won’t be long before it will only require clear verbal commands.
The most advanced general-purpose robots will be shaped like humans because they fit well into a world built for people. Several companies, including Boston Dynamics and Agility Robotics, have designed humanoid robots, and some are being tested in warehouses. Clearly, the plan is to mass produce these bipedal machines, and that’s why Hyundai Motor Co. bought Boston Dynamics in a deal that closed in 2021.
For those worried about intelligent humanoid robots taking everybody’s jobs, there’s no reason to panic. The unmatched dexterity of human hands will keep people useful at least through this century. These early humanoid robots have safety kinks, limited battery life and are somewhat slow and clunky. That shouldn’t stop the debate on how to handle an artificially intelligent machine that can move. The military has shown keen interest in all kinds of ground, sea and air robots. Is it possible to ban ground robots from killing humans? It would be fine to have one carry supplies or help evacuate wounded soldiers. Should they be allowed to be lethal as well?
It may be too late for that debate. Fully autonomous aerial drones are already killing people in Ukraine. The effort by a small group of activists and diplomats failed in an attempt to ban killer robots because the machines are too useful, said Peter Singer, a senior fellow at New America in an April 14 article.
The US must make these humanoid (and canine) robots at home and have a supply chain from the Americas. After inventing the industrial robot, the US failed to mass-produce them, and Japan now dominates the industry with about 46% of industrial robot output. Germany has 6%. The International Federation of Robotics doesn’t break out China’s production level, but it’s large (probably more than 100,000 a year) and growing rapidly. If China fields an army of robots, the US better be able to match.
On the civilian side, it makes sense to require that a human always be responsible for the actions of a robot or several robots. If there’s a glitch in the code or something goes awry, the person in charge should be able to recognize the problem immediately and take corrective action, including disabling the machine. This is straightforward in a factory or warehouse setting. It becomes more complicated when service robots are more developed and interact with the public. Who’s in charge? Should there be a kill switch? Can just anyone pull it?
These questions should be addressed now because robots are dangerous if not handled properly. A Bell Inc. employee was killed by a robot in 2022 while lubricating the rollers on a conveyor belt that formed part of an automated palletiser. The motion of the can of WD-40 over the conveyor triggered the system’s camera and a robotic arm was activated, crushing the 54-year-old worker, according to a report from the Occupational Safety and Health Administration.
Although it may take decades for robots to become sophisticated enough to routinely interact with people, now is the time to lay the groundwork for so-called embodied AI to work safely around humans. It’s a delicate dance because the rules shouldn’t stifle innovation.
No doubt, the marriage of robots and AI will benefit mankind. Robots are tools and will take on even more of the dull, dirty and dangerous jobs now performed by humans, freeing people from repetitive and physically strenuous jobs. But machines can go haywire, and the risks compound as they become more enmeshed in daily life. There must be rules in place to make sure the humans always have the last say.

title: Battling AI Hallucinations : Detect And Defeat False Positives
text:
When we discuss artificial intelligence (AI), we refer to its many advantages – how it accelerates workflows, saves time, and drives better revenues across various fields. It is not wrong by any means. It is driving positive outcomes like never before, but there’s more to the story. AI also has a bad side, one that hallucinates and veers off track from time to time.
When someone using an AI platform starts seeing things that have no connection with reality or facts in any way, it is a case of hallucination. After careful study and research on the subject, one can connect the dots to understand what hallucination is and how to deal with it. But the phenomenon still continues to plague models and affect their adoption, especially in heavily regulated sectors like healthcare.
As a result, despite all the potential AI has to improve medical care and reduce burnout among healthcare professionals, it remains out of reach for many.
AI Adoption Blocked By Hallucinations
Today, medical professionals in many countries use AI platforms like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude to analyze large datasets collected over the years, expedite decision-making, and improve diagnostic accuracy. The language models powering these chatbots can not only process medical scans and reports but also help with medical research, allowing professionals to easily search and understand all knowledge documents easily. Some healthcare providers have exclusively partnered with AI companies to simplify access while focusing on data privacy and control, while others are just scratching the surface with the free products on offer.
But, as these products make their way into healthcare settings, many are also raising alarms over the problems they can lead to. The biggest concern is the risk of hallucinations, where the model can provide incorrect information, ultimately leading to wrong decisions and medical outcomes.
According to GPT-3.5, one of the models powering ChatGPT, hallucinations can be defined as the “generation of content that is not based on real or existing data but is instead produced by a machine learning model’s extrapolation or creative interpretation of data.”
If ignored, hallucinations can have drastic consequences for the healthcare sector worldwide. In fact, healthcare professionals worldwide are already flagging it among the various pitfalls of unhindered usage of generative AI.
For instance, in a recent editorial for Cureus Journal of Medical Sciences, the authors discussed instances of AI-generated misinformation, including producing research papers with fake titles and incorrect PubMed article citations when asked about specific medical conditions. This content, if published, could have easily led unsuspecting individuals into incorrect treatments and decisions.
In a related interview on CBS News' "60 Minutes," Google's developers also spoke on this, acknowledging that while their AI, Gemini, can produce seemingly realistic content, such as book titles, these creations can be inaccurate and not based on real references. They referred to these gaps as "errors with confidence" and emphasized the need for caution and scrutiny when relying on AI-generated information.
How To Address AI Hallucinations?
The understanding of hallucinations, developed over the last few years, has increased focus on the importance of human input and robust oversight when building or using AI for medical purposes. Instead of relying blindly on the information that generative AI has to offer, professionals are looking at keeping the ‘human element’ in the loop. This ensures they get to reap all the benefits AI has on offer without worrying about hallucinations and the generation of misleading information. Many are even using growing ecosystem observability tools in the market to make the monitoring effort easier.
Beyond this, to establish a better grip over hallucinations, organizations should work towards developing education and awareness about AI advancements, including hallucinations and how they are evolving. This way, professionals will have a good idea of what’s happening and stay ahead of the curve to deal with it.
Educational institutes should also start offering “AI in healthcare” courses. This can prepare future doctors and other medical staff to tackle challenges related to misinformation fuelled by AI. If they run into information extracted using generative AI, they will know how to promptly verify it with reliable peer-reviewed sources to avoid any untoward incidences.
Finally, organizations developing AI should focus on improving the accuracy of their data sources. After all, generative AI models are only as good as the data they’re trained upon, serving as high-tech parrots.
In order to do this, clinicians and AI experts must collaborate on an ongoing basis. They should also advocate for more diverse and representative datasets that would better reflect the general population, eliminating the cases of bias and increasing reliability. This synergetic approach will enhance outcomes, strengthen shared decision-making, and ensure AI complements human expertise in the best way possible.
Overall, every stakeholder in the industry needs to recognize that AI is just a tool to make things easier. It should not be treated as a complete replacement. The technology, even though very helpful, still does not possess human qualities — empathy, authority, and ethics – that are critical to successful healthcare systems. There should always be a synergy between AI and humans to tackle the dangers of hallucinations.
The potential of AI, especially in healthcare, is exciting and concerning. These technologies offer possibilities that did not exist previously. Yet, they also raise some valid questions: what to do about the misinformation that they are known to present? Or how to maximize the safety of patients? Unrestrained language models, such as ChatGPT, Gemini, etc., can generate inaccurate outputs, putting the patients at risk. These are still in their embryonic stages, and it will take some time and collaboration to make them truly reliable for use without oversight.
What healthcare professionals need to do now is to ensure responsible behavior when utilizing AI in their research and other tasks. If this path is undertaken, it can help unlock the true potential of these systems while protecting patients and ensuring their well-being.

text:

Japan's Advantest says AI demand boosting memory tester business
Advantest, a manufacturer of chip testing equipment, has been working with HBM since it was first produced in 2013 and is leveraging its relationship with memory makers, Lefever said.
By Sam Nussey
TOKYO: Japan's Advantest said on Wednesday booming demand for high bandwidth memory (HBM) used for artificial intelligence (AI) tasks is boosting its memory tester business.
HBM, a type of high performance memory where chips are stacked to save space and reduce power consumption, is used when processing the large amount of data needed for AI tasks.
"Currently, HBM makes up roughly 50% of our memory testing business and we see that continuing in the near-term," CEO Douglas Lefever said in an interview.
Advantest, a manufacturer of chip testing equipment, has been working with HBM since it was first produced in 2013 and is leveraging its relationship with memory makers, Lefever said.
The equipment maker's share in memory testers grew in the business year ended March and it is forecasting 47% growth in annual sales for the memory segment.
AI and the drive to improve chip performance is leading to increasingly complex combinations of components, which require extensive testing to check performance.
"It will drive the business from the cloud, the data centre ... but then what's really going to turbocharge things will be when those edge applications come out," said Lefever, who took up the post in April.
Edge AI refers to doing AI tasks on local devices rather than in centralised data centres.

title: Council Post: The Role Of Generative AI In Higher Education
text:
Tal Frankfurt is the Founder and CEO of Cloud for Good, a Salesforce partner that creates transformational value with technology.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming all industries, including the nonprofit and educational sectors. In particular, generative AI (GenAI), which includes technologies like generative pre-trained transformers (GPTs), represents a shift in how to approach and execute tasks, offering new opportunities for innovation and efficiency.
Before diving into AI, higher education institutions must clearly define what they aim to achieve. Babson College explained on a recent podcast that they took a thoughtful approach to set up a GenAI pilot for students and faculty, which has grown into a comprehensive generative AI strategy for the college. (Disclosure: Babson College is a Cloud for Good client.) As their Chief Information Officer Patty Patria said, “We are all in on AI.”
Other higher education institutions can learn from Babson's collaborative approach. While not every college is built around the entrepreneurial spirit like Babson, it's important to create a strategy that prioritizes the spirit of learning, risk mitigation, and value creation mindset to provide faculty, staff, and students with the tools and information they need to succeed in the rapidly changing AI landscape. By leveraging a closed AI system, for example, that uses the latest versions of ChatGPT and Dall-E, colleges can successfully integrate AI into their curriculum, administrative operations and, most importantly, their student experience.
Likewise, it's crucial to focus on responsible AI and offering equitable access, which means providing the tools and education the community needs to leverage GenAI.
Having well-defined objectives will guide your AI evaluation process, whether improving operational efficiency, enhancing educational outcomes or better serving the community. Once you have defined your objectives, there are many exciting use cases for GenAI in the nonprofit and education space.
• Some companies are adding AI to existing platforms. Salesforce, for example, announced AI-powered student success tools for their Education Cloud. (Disclosure: Salesforce is a Cloud for Good partner.) This solution now uses AI to analyze program and course information to identify market-relevant skills students will gain and can generate a list that can be added to coursework descriptions. Additionally, this solution can identify available mentors with the right experience to help their mentees, for example, take the next step in their careers.
• Another area where innovation with AI is increasing is advancement. Tools like WealthEngine or Donor Search can enhance donor prospecting by more effectively identifying potential donors. Furthermore, GenAI solutions—such as OpenAI's ChatGPT, Anthrophic's Claude or Salesforce’s Einstein Co-Pilot—can assist in writing personalized donor emails and acknowledgments or even answer questions such as “Will I hit my fundraising goals?” or “What do I need to do to exceed my fundraising goals?”
• Technology partnerships are forming between institutions and the for-profit sector. For example, Arizona State University (ASU) announced its collaboration with OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. Following that partnership, ASU received over 175 proposals from students and faculty for implementing the technology and accepted 105 proposals in three project areas: advancing innovations in teaching and learning, enhancing AI research with social impact, and exploring scaling the public enterprise.
It is important to note that using GenAI public models can raise ethical concerns around bias, transparency and privacy. ChatGPT Enterprise accounts differ from individual ChatGPT licenses in terms of usage scope and data handling. The Enterprise version, which ASU is using, does not expose the data publicly and is not used to train OpenAI models. That said, ChatGPT Enterprise is currently not approved for FERPA-protected data.
It is crucial that before implementing AI models, you create clear policies about how it will be used and what data shouldn’t be inputted or used. Careful planning, ethical considerations and continuous evaluation are key to successfully integrating AI into your nonprofit or educational institution. Embrace these principles to make informed decisions and drive positive change with AI.

title: Council Post: Who Owns AI? Leading Your Organization In AI Implementation Decisions
text:
Marni Carmichael, VP of Marketing, ImageSource Inc.
I recently facilitated a series of regional events with ImageSource customer-partners. Many were state government employees, typically at the director level, whose responsibilities included making technical decisions to improve or replace outdated manual processes. In our conversations, I’ve been impressed with these leaders’ sense of responsibility in spending public funds, their commitment to setting staff up for success, and their focus on building solutions that equally serve constituent requirements and operational needs.
Everyone I talked with shared the goal of streamlining citizen services while reducing back-office manual labor. While they recognized the potential value of artificial intelligence (AI) for reducing process complexity, most expressed uncertainty about which technical choices would best let them leverage current infrastructure while adding new components to improve agency operations.
Since 2023, the public has been overwhelmed by rapidly evolving messaging around AI. Every major technology company (including ImageSource) has an AI-forward position, which every organizational decision-maker experiences as a consumer. AI is everywhere, from ChatGPT or DALL-E’s content generation to Meta’s bafflingly bad search experience. We understand that it can somehow do anything, yet we often don’t see a practical pathway for using AI to solve specific business challenges.
Who truly owns AI, and what roles does it fulfill? This is a particularly important question for leaders in the communications and marketing space to consider. AI represents a conceptual framework for technology that autonomously learns from interaction with humans. It can generate content and make decisions based on existing data and historical patterns. Organizations buy or license AI tools from creators to augment operations—either integrating AI within existing systems or as stand-alone solutions that technical staff can integrate with line-of-business applications. In this sense, the ownership of AI lies with the project champions and technology leaders who guide its implementation and utilization within an organization.
How, then, can leaders guide AI adoption effectively?
Content is the foundation of any AI strategy. If an organization has decent record-keeping, it is already on the path to relevant, useful AI. Digitally organized, metadata-rich content governed by retention policies is ready source material for AI. Even paper files can be used to train AI models with reliable, accessible capture technology. Content migrated from legacy repositories to contemporary infrastructure, such as cloud-based solutions, accelerate AI adoption. Demonstrating the utility of AI through targeted applications, such as AI-powered search engines, enhances stakeholder buy-in and fosters a culture of AI readiness.
A common challenge organizations encounter here is resistance to change. While technology leaders advocate for modernization and the normalization of AI, they may hit walls in the shape of past failed projects or anxiety around operational disruptions. Overcoming these calls for persistent consensus-building, with end users treated as stakeholders and allies. AI champions must maintain transparency regarding challenges and expected outcomes to build trust. Taking an iterative or agile project approach lets the project team identify and resolve challenges rapidly, with frequent progress updates and milestones helping maintain stakeholder engagement and support.
Leaders must become familiar with their organization’s existing tech stack and work within it. If the organization has made new purchases or implementations in the last two years, those providers will likely have AI road maps. Analyzing those projects’ successes or failures will yield an understanding of the risks and challenges likely to impact a new AI implementation. A thorough knowledge of current systems, reevaluating requirements, aligning with stakeholders and proactively managing change can all lead to improved outcomes and adoption success.
The ownership of AI ultimately resides within the organization, with both road bumps and successes marking the ultimate journey toward AI integration. Beginning with manageable datasets and engaging with receptive stakeholders facilitates the first steps to becoming domain experts. For organizational leaders, the journey toward AI implementation demands a blend of technical skills, strategic vision and collaboration to harness this technology’s genuinely transformative potential.

title: Council Post: Boosting Manufacturing Profits: The Impact Of Generative AI
text:
Alice Globus is an industrial AI exec & advisor. Former astrophysicist. Sustainable AI proponent, from semiconductors to data centers.
Managing cost constraints while improving output is always top of mind in the manufacturing sector. Today, corporate leadership is looking to enhance bottom-line efficiencies through the adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI).
AI has already proven itself effective in other tech-heavy domains, such as software development, and it is one of the most viable solutions for manufacturers navigating increasingly challenging circumstances and greater pressure to achieve more with less. Today, manufacturers continue to grapple with many challenges brought about by the pandemic, along with new obstacles, such as U.S. and China relations.
For instance, while supply chain challenges have somewhat eased, the cracks exposed by the pandemic have necessitated manufacturers to enhance resilience, flexibility and reliability. Further, just as raw material prices appeared to be returning to pre-pandemic levels, new disruptions, such as trade restrictions with China, rising interest rates and inflation, have kept the cost of vital supplies elevated.
Although these disruptions may be temporary, they could be indicative of a lasting pattern. In fact, the Boston Consulting Group warns that manufacturers should brace for more "frequent and persistent" supply chain disruptions resulting from political instability, global warming and cross-sector impacts.
In addition to these supply-side challenges, recent data from The Institute for Supply Management shows that demand in the American manufacturing sector has been declining monthly since the fall of 2023. Currently, the manufacturing industry is experiencing a two-and-a-half-year low in new orders.
Despite the myriad challenges, there are also abundant opportunities thanks to significant advances in manufacturing technology, particularly AI. By harnessing a broader array of data and employing powerful machine learning and AI tools capable of identifying patterns and making predictions, manufacturers can realize various potential benefits, including:
• Reducing downtime and defects through predictive maintenance.
• Addressing labor challenges through greater automation.
• Improving quality control through automated inspection.
• Enhancing supply chain optimization and flexibility.
• Improving demand forecasting.
• Enhancing long-term and real-time decision-making.
• Reducing delays and inefficiencies through better production scheduling.
• Lessening waste through green manufacturing practices.
• Improving worker safety.
By embracing AI solutions, manufacturers can identify inefficiencies, vulnerabilities, waste sources and defects more effectively. They can also forecast aspects ranging from supply chain costs to consumer demand to equipment defects more accurately.
In fact, American factories implementing sophisticated AI technologies can achieve an estimated 15% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions, along with a corresponding improvement in maintenance costs by 25%. Furthermore, McKinsey & Company estimates that predictive maintenance can reduce machine downtime by 30%-50% while extending machine life by 20%-40%.
Fully leveraging AI and enjoying its benefits, however, is not without challenges. McKinsey & Company also notes that manufacturers currently collect data from a wide range of sources, resulting in often unusable data due to quality concerns. To harness the most sophisticated AI models, organizations must address data quality issues such as broken sensors, incomplete data mappings, incompatible systems, slow access speeds and insufficient understanding of existing sources. These challenges are further compounded by the demanding environment in which cameras, sensors, machines and other data sources operate.
Improving data quality at scale, coupled with AI algorithms that can put them to use, is among the most effective solutions for enhancing the bottom line in the face of mounting challenges and constraints in the manufacturing sector. Despite the challenges of evolving from legacy systems to those that are purpose-built for the era of AI (and automation is no small feat), it is a necessary transition for improving the bottom line in the face of a mountain of challenges.
Process By Process
Small language models (SMLs) have the potential to ease some of the data challenges encountered within manufacturing by offering efficient and adaptable solutions. These models can analyze and interpret data from various sources, including sensor readings, production logs and maintenance records that provide valuable insights into operational inefficiencies, equipment failures and supply chain disruptions. Through natural language processing (NLP) capabilities, SLMs can parse unstructured data, identify patterns and extract meaningful information, which enhances data quality and usability.
Additionally, SLMs' compact size enables the deployment of edge devices within manufacturing facilities and facilitates real-time analysis and decision-making without relying heavily on centralized computing resources. By leveraging SLMs, manufacturers can streamline data management processes, improve operational efficiency and ultimately enhance their competitive edge in an increasingly complex industrial landscape.

title: Council Post: Hype To Harmony: Integrating Generative AI Into Complete AI Approach
text:
Thomas Robinson is the Chief Operating Officer of Domino Data Lab.
One year and a half after ChatGPT blew away all preconceived notions of where tech was headed, generative AI (GenAI) continues to command executive-level excitement and investment mandates, even among companies that don’t have a clear GenAI strategy.
It’s hard to resist the call when enterprises are expected to double their 2023 investments in GenAI this year from $19 billion worldwide and continue piling on to the tune of $151 billion in 2027. But while some companies are investing in GenAI to lead, and others are doing it to avoid being the caboose, many are putting their money on GenAI simply because it’s the thing to do. Despite perceptions of GenAI advancing beyond the ramp-up phase, Dresner Advisory Services suggests many organizations are still experimenting. Will GenAI meet its high expectations?
Some cracks are certainly starting to show. In the months following ChatGPT’s launch, a slew of new GenAI offerings emerged with many eliciting ante-raising amazement that was certainly earned. But together, they also exposed some technical limitations and adoption challenges, leading more companies to adopt a wait-and-see approach, according to BCG.
But sometimes wisdom is best reserved for the wise. If actions are to be taken on the lessons learned from GenAI’s early days, watching from the sidelines is not one of them.
A Tale Of Two Deployments
In a way, GenAI adoption has been a matter of companies choosing between doing it fast and doing it responsibly. Some companies—tech titans like OpenAI and Google—are deploying new AI models and products at a breakneck pace in a bid for first-to-market dominance. Others are proceeding more cautiously—still innovating, yes—but with transparency, governance, security, privacy and other guardrails baked into every step of the development process. These are the organizations competing in highly regulated industries (finance, life sciences, government, etc.) that have learned to innovate within the most restrictive of parameters—without sacrificing invention or speed. Their understanding of AI is fed by decades of experience and proven by where they sit in the Fortune 100.
While today’s GenAI was just launched over a year ago, these regulated, AI-forward companies bring informed, holistic perspectives on GenAI molded by decades of successfully deploying “traditional” AI to transform their businesses. Unlike many of the organizations whose enthusiasm helps sustain GenAI’s inflated mystique, the true pioneers of AI never saw GenAI as a corporate panacea. They also see the growing disillusionment for what it is: the next natural milestone in GenAI’s journey toward maturity. And they’re currently using GenAI.
Businesses with less AI maturity should take note.
An Exciting But Specialized Addition To The AI Mix
There’s a sense among many of these AI newcomers that they must decide between putting all their money into GenAI or retreating back to predictive and other forms of traditional AI until GenAI earns another look. This should not be an either/or decision.
According to the Gartner article, “Generative AI is only one piece of the much broader AI landscape, and most business problems require a combination of different AI techniques. Ignore this fact, and you risk overestimating the impacts of GenAI and implementing the technology for use cases where it will not deliver the intended results.”
GenAI truly is a transformative tool, but it should be used to elevate an organization’s AI capabilities, not replace them. GenAI exists to serve the use cases that benefit most from what it can do. It works best as part of an integrated mix of AI technologies tailored for specific needs and data contexts.
Indeed, this is the approach many of the chief data and artificial intelligence officers (CIOs) I talk to have adopted. For their traditionally AI-forward companies, updating the AI tech stack to accommodate GenAI was a relatively easy task, requiring a few updates in compute power, data sources and frameworks. They say GenAI accounts for, at most, 15% of their use cases and models. While GenAI surely takes the innovation and business impact of a company’s combined AI capabilities to a new level, predictive AI remains the workhorse in model-driven businesses.
Strategic Alignment Demands A Complete AI Approach
An effective AI strategy is rooted in establishing clear business objectives and use cases. Successful organizations don't implement AI for technology's sake. They do it to address specific pain points, inefficiencies or opportunities where AI can bring real transformation. A financial services firm, for instance, may leverage AI and machine learning to automate credit risk assessments, detect fraud or personalize customer experiences. However, a healthcare provider may use a rules-based system to triage patient symptoms while also deploying an LLM to assist clinicians with drafting personalized treatment plans.
With a custom, integrated approach, organizations can match the AI-driven capability to the need it best serves. With complete AI, there’s also no need to reinvent processes for governance and testing. Predictive AI-powered mortgage risk models require the same rigorous testing, validation and constant monitoring GenAI’s LLM models do.
No AI Strategy Is Complete Without Complete AI
For any technology, a comprehensive and visionary deployment strategy starts with aligning the tech with business goals—not market hype—and upgrading infrastructure and governance while securing the support of leadership. AI is no different, although different forms of AI can solve various problems, and the right combination of AI can solve many problems–in profoundly powerful ways.
The sooner GenAI is seen for what it is, the sooner businesses can value it for what it can do—instead of dismissing it for what it can’t—and putting it to work as part of a larger, complete AI strategy.

title: Council Post: The Key To Government’s Generative AI Success? Bringing In An AI Operator
text:
Eric Velte is ASRC Federal's chief technology officer with 25 years of experience in computer science and technical solutions.
As the federal government continues to explore the seemingly unlimited potential of generative AI, or GenAI, the question of how to regulate the technology supersedes the discussion around its many benefits. The public is skeptical of AI—and for good reason, with so much of the attention on the technology questioning its safety and whether it’s an ethical tool in certain scenarios.
Between the U.S. Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) establishing the U.S. AI Safety Institute Consortium and the U.S. Army strategizing how to promote responsible AI adoption, government leaders continue to prioritize identifying the best practices of AI—and how to limit adversarial threats and algorithmic biases through responsible deployment along the way.
The AI Operator: An Indisputable Asset
As more agencies implement AI for their missions, the government must establish a synergistic relationship between personnel and AI—and quickly. This necessitates a new role, the "AI operator," who can help agencies strike a balance between adopting the tech when and where the agency can benefit from it and ensuring the proper checks and balances exist between the tech and personnel. AI operators would bring a deep understanding of the technology for which they're responsible, helping their organizations adhere to proper risk controls to build and maintain trust with employees and citizens.
An AI operator's role is especially critical when it comes to GenAI. By providing the necessary oversight and comprehensive analysis of current GenAI pilot programs, this role can show decision-makers the tangible benefits of this technology. AI operators can illuminate previously unseen advantages and applications of GenAI, expanding its potential beyond the known use cases.
Leveraging Expertise To Address Challenges
As GenAI's capabilities continue to mature, equipping organizations with dedicated personnel deeply ingrained in the nuances of the technology will be vital to safeguard against security risks, as evidenced by the DOD’s recent announcement of a GenAI task force. Ideal AI operators will possess extensive insight into AI's security challenges, potential biases and ethical implications.
Although GenAI has the potential to significantly optimize agency operations, the federal government must first prepare for its security obstacles before it can reap the benefits. With their sole focus on optimizing the use of GenAI, AI operators would be responsible for guiding the development, training and testing of AI models to intimately understand their weaknesses, like data privacy.
GenAI systems leverage extensive datasets, and federal agencies often face heightened challenges, as they possess sensitive data and information adversaries target. AI operators would devise tailored cybersecurity measures to combat the data challenges GenAI poses and enhance system resilience to mitigate cyberattacks. Additionally, compliance is always a part of the conversation when it comes to emerging technologies. AI operators should be experts in AI regulations and standards to ensure systems comply with federal and industry requirements.
Championing Adoption To Gain Buy-In
Possibly, the most impactful role AI operators can play is as an intermediary between the personnel utilizing the technology in day-to-day operations and the leaders responsible for investing in it. To garner buy-in from leadership, AI operators should not only demonstrate the value of AI adoption but also reduce many of the concerns associated with AI. By highlighting GenAI's strengths, AI operators can appeal to federal leadership and the general public on the advantages of agency GenAI adoption, such as enhanced decision-making, cost savings and improved efficiencies.
Dedicating personnel solely focused on AI could transform how we approach implementation. AI operators bring human perspectives to GenAI by acting as a safeguard during the training and development of AI systems. Infusing GenAI with the human element helps mitigate algorithmic biases and security challenges.
Overall, investing in AI operators could yield substantial returns. Having dedicated AI personnel and a focus on an AI operator at all life cycles mitigates security and ethical risks, helping agencies keep pace with the latest developments of the technology, like GenAI, and ultimately altering the federal landscape by bolstering civilian and leadership buy-in and optimizing use cases.

title: Council Post: Ways AI Can Make Company Data Relevant, Actionable And Impactful
text:
Ab Gaur is the Founder & CEO of Verticurl and also serves as Ogilvy’s Chief Data and Technology Officer.
For most companies, data is both their most valuable resource and abundant asset. It’s also overwhelming in its scope and frequency.
Like a raging river that never runs dry, streams of data inundate companies with incredible knowledge that’s difficult to capture and even more challenging to activate. Like water, these actionable insights slip through their fingers, wasted.
According to one study, 43% of companies “obtain little tangible benefit from their information,” while 23% say they “derive no benefit whatsoever.” One Forrester analysis quantified this loss, finding that “On average, between 60% and 73% of all data within an enterprise goes unused for analytics.”
Simply put, many companies struggle to convert data into meaningful intelligence or actionable insights, which puts them at a competitive disadvantage and prevents them from capitalizing on opportunities to optimize operations, enhance customer experiences and innovate.
The latest breakthroughs in artificial intelligence (AI) for business can help solve this problem.
How AI Restores Structure And Inspires Action
Even as AI experiences an unprecedented hype cycle where its benefits and business implications are often exaggerated to boost stock prices or procure venture capital funding, it is already proficient at taking unruly data sets and making them manageable and insightful, providing a foundation for more accurate decision-making and timely innovation.
AI technologies, particularly machine learning and deep learning, are at the forefront of enabling businesses to sift through massive datasets to identify patterns, trends and anomalies. More specifically, these technologies excel at converting expansive amounts of unstructured data into structured data that can yield meaningful results.
In this case, AI isn’t breaking new ground. It’s getting better at performing tasks it has excelled at for years.
For instance, in 2020, the MIT Sloan Management Review reported, “Artificial intelligence has been applied successfully in thousands of ways, but one of the less visible and less dramatic ones is in improving data management.” The publication identified five ways AI excels at data management, including classification, cataloging, quality, security and data integration.
Of course, knowing what this technology can do differs from knowing how to apply it to your business.
Brands are racing to bridge that gap.
Best Practices For Activating Data With AI
Less than two years after Open AI’s ChatGPT brought AI to the forefront of the public consciousness (though the technology existed before the company released this product), 73% of companies have adopted AI in some business areas.
It’s a learning experience that will differentiate truly data-driven, forward-leaning companies from their less adaptive counterparts.
Here are three best practices for activating the power of cloud data using the latest AI technologies.
#1 Customize Marketing Outreach
Effective marketing is predicated on meeting customers where they are, delivering the right pitch and solving the right problem at the right time.
AI makes this more possible and practical than ever before.
By analyzing custom data, including past customer interactions, website visits and email engagement data, brands can produce predictive engagement scoring.
These predictive scores indicate customers’ probability of engaging with future campaigns.
Equipped with this information, marketers can create more precise audience segmentation to deliver more personalized content and offers across channels that matter most to their customers.
#2 Prioritize Lead Efficiency
AI can efficiently assess various lead characteristics, accurately identifying key traits such as industry, company size and engagement history.
These insights let brands be more efficient with their leads, forecasting the likelihood of conversion so resources and assets are deployed appropriately, concentrating on targeting prospects with a higher probability of closing deals.
#3 Simplify Segment Generation
AI gives marketers the ability to quickly create audience segments and refine targeting using natural language queries of company data.
When coupled with AI-powered recommendations, they can generate effective market segments to maximize campaign impact.
By making data understandable, searchable and usable, marketers can simplify segmentation at scale.
Doing Better Work With Data
It’s reasonable to assume that today’s AI systems are as bad as they are ever going to be.
For businesses, this means that its ability to decode complex datasets in real time has the potential to drive better business outcomes for the foreseeable future.
As a result, AI is quickly becoming indispensable for companies looking to leverage their data as a strategic asset.

title: Council Post: What's Next For AI And Video: From Trusting Your Eyes To The Labor Market
text:
Chris Savage, CEO and cofounder of Wistia.
In a world filled with AI, how can we be sure job candidates are who they say they are? How can we know they’re not using bots to answer interview questions? What happens to trust when more companies start using AI-directed interviews themselves?
These are very real concerns a teammate, and I recently grappled with. This world is coming, and I think we’ll start seeing more old-school, in-person interviews as a result.
We're living through the most exciting tech evolution we’ve ever seen because of advances in AI. We need to think ahead and consider the potential implications of this technology.
AI is affecting trust, transforming the labor market and influencing content quality. Here’s why.
Trust As A Valuable Currency
Hiring is just one example of how AI is eroding trust. The use of deepfake videos may be the most unnerving of all. Almost anyone can pose as someone else behind an AI headshot. We may begin to see more imperfect “real” videos of people as a result. After all, you’re more likely to trust a clip of humans walking down the street and interacting with one another than a video of a talking head, right?
If you're making a big, external buying decision, I wouldn't be surprised to see a large increase in in-person meetings or interactions to help instill more trust. I think we’ll also begin to rely even more on recommendations, reviews and word of mouth, especially from people we actually know.
Trust is critical to business success and needs to be earned. To earn trust, the in-person connection needs to be prioritized more than ever before. Build in more time and processes to foster increased trust through in-person meetings, interactions and collaboration.
A Changing Labor Market
Debates around AI’s impact on jobs aren't new. But we’re seeing some interesting trends unfold within our current economic landscape.
In the tech industry, hiring practices are tightening because of stock market pressure. Meanwhile, AI is already impacting more entry-level jobs like copywriting and coding. Some predict that AI could replace over half (56%) of entry-level positions in the next five years. So, we can expect significant shifts in the labor market and much unpredictability.
However, human involvement will continue to be necessary for many jobs, as AI still hasn’t matched human judgment or emotion and, unfortunately, has human biases. So, there’s the question of whether AI will actually replace most jobs or just dramatically change what those jobs are. We may see some instances where the percentage of people working in a role may actually increase with AI, but the work they're doing may change.
Businesses need to implement hiring and talent retention systems that recognize this possibility and the importance of enhancing the human touch, not replacing it.
Increasing Content Quality
Right now, almost anyone can use AI to create videos and other content for consumption, which is great from a creative expression standpoint. My team and I have fun all the time experimenting internally with these tools. But it also means there's a larger volume of “average” content being fed to consumers.
Average content won’t move the needle for companies. It can be impersonal, lacking in strategy and gets lost in the noise. Rise above average by being more human and authentic in all the content you produce. Make sure your content is helpful and solves customers’ problems.
To do this, you can establish new systems to review content quality before it goes public. Integrate customer feedback loops to ensure content effectively meets audience needs. This is what will set you apart, especially as consumer expectations rise.
When it comes to the video industry, in particular, video quality needs to improve to stand out. I can envision us ending up in a world with a smaller number of big video hits. That’s because AI can't replicate the art it takes to make a video: its pacing, the storytelling and the art of evoking emotion. This is a true skill reserved for some of the most talented (and human) production teams. This authenticity is key to driving more engagement and business success.
AI is taking each of us on a long and wild ride. Every day, we hear about more AI advancements, success stories and failures. I’ve experimented with many of them (and even failed). We’ll continue to experience its many upsides and downsides.
There’s no way to predict how AI will shape our lives over the next five or 10 years. But we can all do our best to stay ahead of its evolving trends and harness its power by ensuring we have the right systems in place to maintain integrity. If you can master the art of maintaining trust in these unprecedented times, you might unlock the key to winning big.

title: Good News For Human Beings - AI Doesn’t Do Judgment
text:
By Sir Andrew Likierman, Professor of Management Practice in Accounting
The evidence of artificial intelligence's (AI) presence is all around us.
To illustrate, let’s go shopping. The barcodes being swiped through the tills may mark the end of our weekly visit, but they are raw material for AI.
Stock control programs using Big Data on weather and demand trends combine with our swipe to get the right replacement products onto the shelves. Meanwhile, increasingly sophisticated cameras track purchases and help to identify potential shoplifters. Behind the scenes, AI programs in Head Office model strategy, market trends, financial planning and much more.
This is a long way from the friendly local store, where there is a personal response to each visit and each transaction. Ordering, stocking, keeping theft down and income up is all down to the shopkeeper. No wonder the march of AI is seen as dehumanising, even apocalyptic.
But this apparently straight replacement of the cheerful shopkeeper by dehumanised AI plays more to our fears of what is being substituted than the reality. AI needs humans to set goals (or the tasks for programs without goals), write the programs, train the data, check data quality and interpret the results.
'Garbage in' remains 'garbage out' and, in a fast-moving world, human judgment is required to keep the garbage out and make sense of what the machine tells us. That includes the answers we get from ChatGPT. Without human judgment, Big Data is just Big Numbers.
So what is it that machines can’t do that we humans can in exercising judgment?
Machines:
- don’t have consciousness or intentionality;
- cannot think abstractly or form an opinion;
- are not good at identifying relevance through context (the appropriate comment in one situation or culture which is deeply offensive in another) and they don’t “do” meaning (think metaphor, irony, or sense of humour);
- don’t have belief nor conscience through ethics and spirituality, or self-belief through aspiration or ambition;
- don’t have emotion or empathy and can’t create relationships or other social bonds involving feeling;
- can’t anticipate spontaneity, idiosyncrasy, contextual shifts, or fallibility; and
- cannot remedy incompleteness, including the confusion of correlation with causation.
That’s quite a list. Moving on from shop-keeping, all the major judgments we have to make in our working and personal lives include some combination of them. Dealing with colleagues, competitors, climate change or children involve most.
To pin 'judgment' down, it’s the combination of relevant knowledge and experience with personal qualities to make decisions and form opinions.
We exercise it by the awareness we have, in knowing who and what to trust, in understanding our feelings and beliefs, by the way we make our choice and, in the case of decisions, by being able to deliver what we have chosen. (For those interested, I describe the framework in detail in my article 'The Elements of Good Judgment' in the Harvard Business Review January/February 2020).
So, whatever a machine does through AI, it does not exercise judgement – machines are not mechanical human beings. Even the disputed possibility of 'General Artificial Intelligence', where what the machine can do equals what the human can, does not fill these gaps.
These reasons do not mean that humans are better than machines in all situations. On the contrary, there may well be relative strengths and weaknesses in using machines. The comparative superiority of the machine comes in some cases from human weakness. AI provides speed and consistency, neutrality and focus, while not being bored, ill, temperamental, carried away by greed and fear, or by algorithms having distracting love affairs with each other.
The assumption that there is universal substitution is, in any case, simplistic.
Dr Eric Topol, in his book Deep Medicine, describes the superiority of AI over humans in some medical specialties such as radiology, where human fallibility is an issue. AI is even better at some aspects of nursing as a result of remote monitoring of patients at home.
But AI cannot provide “the power of detailed, careful observation”, especially with complex and psychological support, not only in nursing but all aspects of medicine. Topol believes that the ideal is humans and machines working together, with machines freeing humans to do what they do best – talking to patients.
AI is not a zero-sum game where machines gain and humans lose. As illustrated in Deep Medicine, it will be the combination of the machine and the human being that provides quality medical care.
Those who fail to recognise what AI can and cannot offer will be outflanked by those who do. But far from diminishing the role of judgement, AI will make the central contribution of human beings even clearer in choices combining permutations of situations without a precedent, significant complexity, new variables, abstract thinking, unusual trade-offs, insufficient data, convoluted qualitative factors, multidimensional risk, idiosyncratic relationships, and the nuances of personality.
In other words, most of what senior managers do and the reason they are paid handsomely to do it.
Sir Andrew Likierman is Professor of Management Practice in Accounting at London Business School. His current research is on human judgment. He has published on judgment in leadership, on the board, in professions and in managing during Covid-19. Sir Likierman has advised the UK's House of Commons Treasury, Employment, Transport and Social Services Select Committees. He is a past President of the Chartered Institute of Management Accountants and was a member of the Financial Reporting Council. In the field of corporate governance, he was a member of the Cadbury Committee on UK corporate governance, and of the steering committee set up by Secretary-General Kofi Annan on the governance of the United Nations.

title: Council Post: How To Responsibly Adapt To Artificial Intelligence In AppSec
text:
Sandeep Johri is CEO of Checkmarx, a leader in enterprise-native cloud application security.
Over the years, there have been many disruptive technologies that changed the nature of how we do business or even how we operate as a society. Think of things like ride-sharing apps, streaming video and the Internet of Things (IoT)—even the internet itself. While these phenomena are each still evolving and shifting our world, none may be as much at the forefront of change today as AI. In fact, some even suggest that AI is the disruptor of the century.
2023 was undeniably AI’s breakout year, but what amazes me most about the new technology isn’t the surge in adoption—it’s how developers feel about it and what that means for businesses. Reports show that 42% of developers trust the output that is coming out of AI. That leaves 58% rightfully skeptical.
After all, can we accurately predict what this evolving technology and emerging tools mean for enterprises? What does it all mean for AppSec managers and developers? And how can we figure out the best approach to leveraging this technology and navigating the AI tsunami of risks and benefits?
First, we must understand what these risks and benefits are.
AI has entered and disrupted the AppSec chat.
AI is disrupting application security—and software development in general—in three main ways.
First, the way that software developers work is changing. In the past, most of the source code was written from scratch by developers. Now, with AI, we see a shift toward code being generated by generative AI (GenAI) assistants. AI can save developers a lot of time, but can we trust that the code it generates is free of vulnerabilities that threat actors can exploit to bring about data breaches and cyberattacks? Definitely not.
To effectively mitigate the risks posed by unexpected AI-generated vulnerabilities in a time-pressured development environment, we need to prioritize safeguarding the code at its source. This involves implementing protective measures directly within the AI tools and dashboards that developers use.
Beyond this initial step, continuous testing and protection must be maintained throughout the entire development process, from the moment coding begins until the application goes live in the cloud. This is also known as code-to-cloud security.
Second, as with any new technology, AI brings completely new types of risks and attacks. Last year, my own security researchers saw several new types of attacks, with the most interesting of them being "AI hallucinations." Many software developers incorporate software packages from open-source libraries to save time, but what happens when threat actors "poison" that library of software packages?
They found that software developers using ChatGPT to generate code were receiving instructions to install software packages that could install malicious packages, or packages poisoned with viruses, all while believing the packages were legitimate and safe.
The third and final example of how AI is disrupting the application security industry can be seen in the way that many vendors, including us, have begun embedding secure AI solutions to help their enterprise customers learn their software solutions quickly and more effectively.
What skills will be most valuable in an AI-enhanced future for AppSec?
I believe that AI-enabled workers will replace workers not enabled with AI. I think the biggest challenge in upskilling is that we are battling a constantly moving target. The rapid pace of technological change makes it difficult for organizations to stay ahead and effectively manage investments. This means there is always something new you must be learning and teaching to your organization.
To prepare your workforce for AI integration, you should focus on continuous learning and adaptability, including upskilling in areas like data analysis, AI ethics and human-AI collaboration. I believe critical thinking, creativity and emotional intelligence will be invaluable skills, as they complement AI capabilities and are essential for innovation and effective decision-making in an AI-enhanced future.
So how can AppSec teams adapt?
In the application security industry, AI introduces ethical considerations around data privacy, bias in AI algorithms and the security of AI systems. As CEO, I’ve directed my team to tackle these concerns by implementing data governance policies to ensure privacy and consent; conducting regular audits and updates to algorithms to minimize bias; and enhancing security protocols to protect against AI vulnerabilities.
We also prioritize transparency with stakeholders about how AI is used and its implications, and we invest in continuous education for our team on AI best practices to ensure we're developing responsibly. These are all things you can do in your organizations as well.
In every discussion that we have with our customers, AI is raised as a top concern. Enterprises need help to understand the risk and are looking for advice from their security partners on what to do and, most importantly, what not to do. The main impact on code generators is that we’re about to see the volume of code being generated increase exponentially, while security tools and staff will continue to increase linearly. Vendors must help their customers to close the gaps and continue to deliver their best innovations.
We know that open-source AI models pose a danger of concealing malicious code. Additionally, research indicates that developers using AI assistants are more likely to believe their code is secure compared to those without such tools. While AI has the potential to enhance developer productivity, it also introduces new challenges to the development process, making it a critical consideration for AppSec.
With all of that said, achieving success with AI requires surveilling the AI landscape, aligning it with specific needs and challenges and understanding potential pitfalls.

title: Council Post: Navigating The Challenges Of Generative AI In Software Development
text:
Ankit Virmani is an ethical AI and data engineering expert at Google focused on customers' successful data and machine learning journeys.
The integration of generative AI, specifically large language models (LLMs), into software development processes presents a myriad of opportunities for enhancing productivity and innovation. However, technology leaders must also navigate the challenges that arise from using these powerful tools. This article explores the key challenges associated with using generative AI in software development and provides practical strategies for circumventing these obstacles, drawing on real-world examples.
1. Code Quality And Reliability
One of the primary challenges of using generative AI in software development is ensuring the quality and reliability of the generated code. While LLMs can produce syntactically correct code, they may not always generate functionally correct or optimized solutions. If left unchecked, this can lead to bugs, security vulnerabilities and performance issues.
Example: A development team at a financial institution used an LLM to generate code for a critical trading system. While the generated code compiled successfully, it contained subtle logical errors that caused incorrect calculations and potential financial losses. The team had to spend significant time debugging and fixing the generated code.
Strategy: Technology leaders should establish rigorous testing and code review processes to mitigate this challenge. Developers should treat AI-generated code as a starting point and subject it to comprehensive unit testing, integration testing and code reviews. Implementing static code analysis tools and continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipelines can help catch quality issues early in the development cycle.
2. Bias And Fairness
Generative AI models, including LLMs, can inherit biases and discriminatory patterns from the data on which they are trained. These biases can propagate into the generated code if not addressed, leading to unfair or discriminatory outcomes.
Example: An e-commerce company used an LLM to generate product recommendation algorithms. However, the generated code exhibited biases based on gender and race, resulting in skewed recommendations that favored certain demographics over others. This bias led to customer complaints and reputational damage for the company.
Strategy: Technology leaders must prioritize fairness and bias mitigation when using generative AI. This involves carefully curating training data to ensure diversity and representativeness, conducting regular fairness audits and implementing bias detection and mitigation techniques. Collaborating with ethicists and diverse stakeholders can help identify and address potential biases early in the development process.
3. Intellectual Property And Attribution
The use of generative AI in software development raises questions about intellectual property rights and proper attribution. As LLMs generate code based on patterns learned from existing codebases, there may be ambiguity regarding the ownership and licensing of the generated code.
Example: A startup used an LLM to generate a significant portion of its codebase. However, when seeking funding, investors raised concerns about the generated code's intellectual property rights and the potential legal risks associated with using AI-generated code without proper attribution.
Strategy: Technology leaders should establish clear policies and guidelines for using generative AI in software development. This includes defining ownership and licensing models for AI-generated code, ensuring compliance with open-source licenses and implementing proper attribution mechanisms. Consulting with legal experts specializing in intellectual property and AI can help navigate these complex issues.
4. Skill Development And Workforce Adaptation
The adoption of generative AI in software development may require developers to acquire new skills and adapt to new workflows. Some developers may feel threatened by AI's potential to automate certain tasks and fear job displacement.
Example: A software development company introduced an LLM-based code generation tool to improve productivity. However, some senior developers resisted using the tool, fearing that it would make their expertise obsolete and lead to job losses.
Strategy: Technology leaders should approach the integration of generative AI as an opportunity to upskill and empower developers. Providing training and education programs on how to effectively leverage AI tools can help developers adapt to the changing landscape. Emphasizing the role of human expertise in problem-solving, system design and creativity can alleviate concerns about job displacement. Fostering a culture of collaboration and continuous learning can help developers embrace AI as a valuable tool rather than a threat.
5. Explainability And Transparency
The decision-making processes of generative AI models can be opaque, making it challenging to understand how they arrive at specific code suggestions or decisions. This lack of explainability and transparency can be problematic, especially in regulated industries or when dealing with sensitive data.
Example: A healthcare software company used an LLM to generate code for patient data analysis. However, when audited by regulatory authorities, the company struggled to explain how the generated code processed and protected patient data, leading to compliance issues and potential fines.
Strategy: Technology leaders should prioritize explainability and transparency when using generative AI in software development. Collaborating with AI researchers and vendors to develop explainable AI techniques can help provide insights into the reasoning behind generated code. Implementing logging and auditing mechanisms can track the use of AI-generated code and ensure accountability. Regularly communicating the limitations and uncertainties associated with generative AI to stakeholders can help set appropriate expectations.
Conclusion
The use of generative AI in software development presents both opportunities and challenges for technology leaders. Organizations can harness the power of generative AI while mitigating potential risks by proactively addressing issues such as code quality, bias, intellectual property, skill development and explainability. Establishing responsible AI practices, fostering a culture of collaboration between humans and AI, and continuously learning and adapting to new technologies will be crucial for success in the era of AI-assisted software development. By navigating these challenges strategically, technology leaders can unlock the full potential of generative AI and drive innovation in the software development industry.
